problem: Generic deep RNN/LSTM policies fail to learn navigation under partial observability because their priors ignore the sequential structure of planning, while model-based POMDP methods need hand-built or hard-to-learn models. Prior differentiable planners either assume full observability or only do state estimation, and QMDP-nets were limited to simplified domains.
motivation: Real robots must localize from noisy visual observations on a 2D floor map, plan, and avoid unforeseen obstacles, all without knowing their start location. Embedding a planning algorithm as a differentiable program lets the model be learned end-to-end and avoids the difficulty of conventional model learning. The goal is to scale algorithmic priors to large, visual 3D domains.
key_idea: Encode the whole navigation pipeline (Bayesian histogram filter, QMDP planner, reactive actor) as a single end-to-end trainable recurrent network whose weights are a learned POMDP model conditioned on the floor map.
insight: Training end-to-end lets the network learn a POMDP model that compensates for the approximate QMDP planner, so NavNet beats the clairvoyant QMDP expert that generated its demonstrations (97.5% vs 81.1% on Task A, 91.5% vs 62.6% on Task C). This only holds when training on successful demonstrations: when unsuccessful demonstrations were also included, NavNet did not beat QMDP. Direct comparisons with unstructured DNNs were deferred, so the value of the algorithmic priors is argued from prior QMDP-net reports rather than ablated here.
method: Bayesian filter layer: histogram belief over a 19x19 grid x 4 orientations; the transition update is a 3x3 convolution with L·|A| channels, and the observation update is a multiplication followed by normalization.

Learned observation model: a CNN maps the 60x80 RGB image and the floor map to the unnormalized conditional z(s)=p(s|o_t,map), used directly in the belief update instead of learning the joint Z(s,o|map).
QMDP planner layer: K steps of value iteration implemented as conv and max-pool layers, with a learned reward CNN over the map; action values q(a)=sum_s Q_K(s,a)b(s).

Reactive actor: takes the current image and a plan vector (q values plus 4 past q vectors and 4 past actions) and outputs a low-level action, allowing deviation from the plan to avoid unforeseen obstacles.

Training: behavior cloning with a cross-entropy loss via BPTT, with no supervision on POMDP components. Demonstrations are successful clairvoyant QMDP trajectories in 10k random environments (5 each). Curriculum: synthetic binary-observation grids, then Task A, B, C.

setting.backbone: NavNet: differentiable Bayesian filter + QMDP planner + CNN/FC actor (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: 10k random Unity3D environments, 5 successful clairvoyant-QMDP expert trajectories each, plus a synthetic-grid curriculum stage
setting.observation: monocular RGB 60x80 + 19x19 binary 2D floor map; unknown start pose
setting.action_space: discrete grid actions: forward, turn left, turn right, stay
setting.simulator: custom Unity 3D-based simulator (random layouts, 23 furniture types)
setting.privileged: none at test time (the expert used for training data has full map and occupancy observations)

numbers.extra: walls-only map, objects are non-colliding visual obstruction; trained by imitation of clairvoyant QMDP
map includes all objects, all objects collide
map shows walls only, all objects collide; full architecture with reactive actor

numbers_note: Custom simulator benchmark only; no standard benchmarks. Results are preliminary, with no ablations against other DNN architectures.
results: NavNets reach the goal in 97.5%, 96.5% and 91.5% of unseen environments on Tasks A, B and C, beating the clairvoyant QMDP expert (81.1%, 84.1%, 62.6%). Task C still has a 14.5% collision rate, which is unsatisfactory for real use.
limitations: Task C collision rate (14.5%) is too high, because the actor is memoryless and only sees the immediate next plan value.
Only preliminary experiments in a simulated discrete 19x19 grid with discrete actions; no real robot and no direct comparison with other DNN architectures.
The histogram belief and repeated planning computation limit scaling to high-dimensional states.
